title: MindFlow: Mind Supernet Powered Thinking Flows for Research Idea Innovation
claim: Prior methods rely on predefined, static multi-stage pipelines; ours samples flexible, optimizable flows from a supernet to meet open-ended, multi-objective challenges.
layout: 3 dashed panels: challenges on top, prior vs ours below; sad/happy faces
description: The figure has three dashed-border rounded panels on a cream background. The top panel presents two challenges. Challenge 1, "open-ended", shows a laptop with a question mark plus a jigsaw puzzle, labeled problem-finding and problem-solving. Challenge 2, "multi-objective", shows two balance scales weighing labeled balls A to D (effectiveness, novelty, significance, feasibility), captioned "Trade-off!". The bottom-left panel, "Recent works" with a sad face, shows a vertical chain of gray nodes: background context, propose design and solution, final idea. It includes a loop for iterative novelty boosting and snowflake icons for frozen stages. It ends with the red text "Predefined, Static pipeline!". The bottom-right panel, "MindFlow" with a happy face, shows a grid of colored operator nodes (Mind Supernet) with flame icons. Arrows lead to two sampled Thinking Flow subgraphs. It ends with the red text "Explicit, controllable, optimizable!". The eye goes first to the bold blue and red headings.
caption: Overview of challenges in research idea generation and comparison between prior pipelines and MindFlow.
abstract: Research idea innovation is a fundamental engine of scientific progress, yet it remains difficult to generate and evaluate in a scalable and controllable way. This challenge lies in its inherently open-ended and multi-objective nature, where ideas should balance novelty, plausibility and feasibility. While recent LLM-based approaches have made progress through carefully designed prompts or agent pipelines, they are constrained by predefined, static ideation workflows. To address this limitation, we propose MindFlow, a framework that explicitly formulates ideation as a graph-structured Flow in Mind, which is composed of modular thinking operators and modeled by a probabilistic mind supernet. Given a research topic, a controller dynamically samples thinking flows to generate candidate ideas. This open-ended problem is optimized using a tournament-based relative ranking, enabling the controller to progressively favor higher-quality thinking flows. We further introduce an evaluation protocol that jointly assesses problem finding and problem solving, going beyond title- or abstractonly judgments. Across diverse topics, MindFlow shows its superiority as an explicit, controllable and optimizable research idea innovator.
